name: Laozi
info: Laozi, the 'Old Master', is the figure traditionally held to be the author of the Tao Te Ching and the founder of Taoism; scholars doubt that he lived as the tradition tells, and the book is generally seen as the work of several hands.

facts.born: In the village of Quren in the state of Chu, present-day Luyi in Henan, as the traditional accounts have it, in the 6th century BCE; the son of the Censor-in-Chief of the Zhou dynasty and Lady Yishou
facts.died: Not recorded; in the best-known account he departed west through a frontier gate at the age of 80, and some religious traditions hold that he became an immortal hermit
facts.role: Keeper of the Archives for the royal Zhou court in the tradition; regarded by Taoists as the founder of the faith and, in some sects, as a god; historians treat him as a figure of doubtful historicity
facts.known: the Tao Te Ching (Dào Dé Jīng); the idea of wu wei; the encounter with Confucius; the departure to the west; the ancestor of the Tang dynasty's rulers; the founding figure of Taoism

t: Laozi, meaning 'Old Master', is an honorific and not a personal name; the traditional accounts name him Li Er and describe him as a keeper of the archives at the Zhou court.
By the mid-twentieth century most Western scholars regarded his historicity as doubtful and the Tao Te Ching as a compilation by many hands.
The book teaches the Tao and wu wei, and Laozi became a god in later Taoism and an imperial ancestor under the Tang.
dyk: Taoist myths say that Laozi was conceived when his mother gazed upon a falling star, remained in her womb for 62 years and was born as a grown man with a full grey beard while she leaned against a plum tree.
ev: Traditional accounts place the birth of Laozi, as Li Er, in the state of Chu
The oldest manuscript containing text from the Dào Dé Jīng, on bamboo slips, is written
The oldest complete manuscripts of the Dào Dé Jīng are placed in a tomb at Mawangdui
Sima Qian writes the earliest biographical reference to Laozi in his Records of the Grand Historian
Emperor Gaozong gives Laozi the first of a series of grand temple names
Emperor Xuanzong declares Laozi the Sage Ancestor of the Tang dynasty
Laozi is honoured with the longest of his Tang titles

sections.early:
Lǎozǐ is not a personal name but an honorific title, essentially 'old teacher' or 'venerable master', built like Kongzi (Confucius), Mengzi and Zhuangzi. Traditional accounts give him the personal name Li Er, and he has long been identified with Lao Dan. His courtesy name is recorded as Boyang. A legend ties his birth to a plum tree, and the surname Li also means 'plum'.

The earliest biographical reference is in the Records of the Grand Historian by Sima Qian, written in the 1st century BCE, who presents several accounts of Laozi and expresses varying doubt about his sources. In one, Laozi was a contemporary of Confucius in the 6th or 5th century BCE, born in the village of Quren in the southern state of Chu, within present-day Luyi in Henan. He was the son of the Censor-in-Chief of the Zhou dynasty and Lady Yishou, and a scholar who worked as Keeper of the Archives at the royal Zhou court, which reportedly gave him wide access to the works of the Yellow Emperor and other classics.

By the mid-twentieth century, a consensus had emerged among Western scholars that the historicity of a person known as Laozi is doubtful. The rest of this page tells the life as the tradition tells it.
sections.rise:
The sources say little of how Laozi came to prominence, and the accounts differ on who he was. In the first, he served at the Zhou court at Wangcheng, modern Luoyang, as royal archivist. In a second, he was a different contemporary of Confucius called Lao Laizi, one of the Twenty-four Filial Exemplars, who wrote a book in 15 parts. In a third, he was the court astrologer Lao Dan, who lived in the 4th century BCE during the reign of Duke Xian of Qin, grew weary of the moral decay of life in Chengzhou and noted the kingdom's decline.

In the Confucian tradition he met and impressed Confucius. There are many variations of the story of their encounter, most famously in the Zhuangzi. A. C. Graham suggested that the version in the Book of Rites was the original, borrowed and reinterpreted by the followers of Zhuang Zhou.

The stories assert that Laozi never opened a formal school but nonetheless attracted many students and loyal disciples. His birthday is popularly held to be the 15th day of the second month of the Chinese calendar. Where he is said to have married, he had a son who became a celebrated soldier of Wei during the Warring States period.
sections.deeds:
The work attributed to him is the Dào Dé Jīng, often called the Laozi. In the best-known story, Lao Dan set out west at the age of 80 to live as a hermit in the unsettled frontier. At the western gate the guard Yinxi recognised him and asked him to record his wisdom for the good of the country before he would be allowed to pass. The text Laozi wrote is said to be the Dào Dé Jīng, though the present version includes additions from later periods.

The book describes the Tao as the source and ideal of all existence: unseen but not transcendent, immensely powerful yet humble, the root of all things. It aims to lead its students to a return to their natural state in harmony with the Tao, and it treats language and conventional wisdom as biased and artificial, often using paradox. Wu wei, 'non-action', is a central concept, and it can mean not forcing, acting spontaneously or flowing with the moment. In politics it means avoiding war, harsh laws and heavy taxes. Unlike most works of its kind, the book has no central master figure and seldom mentions historical people or events, which gives it an air of timelessness. Its ideas are explained by paradox, analogy, repetition, symmetry, rhyme and rhythm. Alan Chan reads it as urging a return to nature and to the calm of wu wei, free from desire, in place of a false sense of progress through technology.
sections.opponents:
The sources record no opponent of Laozi in his own time. The disputes concern the man and the book. Sima Qian presents multiple accounts of his life with varying levels of doubt. In the 20th century, textual criticism led to theories questioning Laozi's date or even his existence and proposing that the received Dào Dé Jīng was composed no earlier than the Warring States period, by several authors.

The manuscripts bear on the question. The oldest, written on bamboo slips from Guodian in the late 4th century BCE, hold passages corresponding to roughly a third of the received text, mixed with passages that the transmitted version lacks, which suggests that the text was still being revised. The oldest complete manuscripts, from a tomb at Mawangdui, date to the early 2nd century BCE. Analysis of early commentary supports a gradual growth of the text rather than a single act of authorship.

The readings of the book are also contested. Its advice that rulers keep their people 'simple-minded' has been explained as a call for calm free from desires, though some scholars say this ignores the religious context and others call it an apology for the text's coherence. Roderick Long argues that libertarian themes in Taoist thought were borrowed from earlier Confucian writers.
sections.last:
The traditions give no death. In the best-known account, once Yinxi had his text Laozi passed through the gate and was not recorded again. In some versions the guard was so touched by the work that he became a disciple and left with him, never to be seen again. In some later interpretations the Old Master travelled all the way to India and taught Siddartha Gautama, the Buddha, and others say that he was the Buddha himself.

Religious Taoism often holds that Laozi did not vanish after writing the Dào Dé Jīng but spent his life travelling and revealing the Tao. In some sects of Taoism, Chinese Buddhism, Confucianism and Chinese folk religion it is held that he became an immortal hermit. Taoist myths say that he was reborn 13 times after his first life in the days of Fuxi and that in his last incarnation as Laozi he lived 990 years.

Some versions of the story give him a son, a celebrated soldier of Wei. In the Siddhar tradition of India, Bhogar, one of the 18 revered Siddhars, is believed to be Laozi. His jeeva samadhi is said to be in the Dhandayuthapani Swamy Temple at Palani in Tamil Nadu.
sections.legacy:
Laozi is generally considered the founder of Taoism. Since the Han dynasty his story has taken on religious overtones: he was worshipped as a god, and belief in the revelation of the Tao from the divine Laozi led to the Way of the Celestial Masters, the first organised religious Taoist sect. Certain devotees held the Dào Dé Jīng to be the avatar, in the form of a book, of the god Laojun, one of the Three Pure Ones. A seventh-century work, the Sandong Zhunang, presents Laozi as the perfect Taoist master and Yinxi as the ideal student.

Because of the name Li Er he was venerated as the ancestor of all Lis, including the emperors of the Tang dynasty, and is honoured in modern China as the progenitor of the surname Li. Under the Tang his titles grew: in 666 Emperor Gaozong gave him the first of a series of titles of increasing grandeur, in 743 Emperor Xuanzong declared him the Sage Ancestor of the dynasty and raised his parents to imperial rank, and further honours followed in 749 and 754.

Officials in Chinese history drew on Laozi and Zhuangzi to refuse service to any ruler. Modern writers have read him as a proponent of limited government: Murray Rothbard called him the first libertarian, and Rudolf Rocker, Peter Kropotkin and Ursula K. Le Guin have written of his links with anarchism.

summary: Laozi, the Old Master, is the traditional author of the Tao Te Ching and founder of Taoism. Scholars doubt that he lived as the tradition tells and see the book as the work of many hands; later religion made him a god and an ancestor of the Tang emperors.

Holmes Hinkley Jr. Welch, Taoism: The Parting of the Way (Beacon Press, 1957)
Roel Sterckx, Ways of Heaven: An Introduction to Chinese Thought (Basic Books, 2019)
